messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis

Details: The issue stems from the method sample(int sampleSize) in the DiscreteDistribution class. This method attempts to create an array of generic type T using reflection by calling:

```java
(T[]) java.lang.reflect.Array.newInstance(singletons.get(0).getClass(), sampleSize);
```

This line assumes that the class of the first element in the singletons list is the exact runtime type for the generic type T. However, if this first element is of a subtype T1 of T, and during sampling sample() produces instances of T that are not of subtype T1, the array creation and subsequent assignment will fail with an ArrayStoreException.

In the failing test `testIssue942`, two objects are added as keys in a list of pairs, both of subtype Object but as anonymous classes (thus each new Object() {} is a distinct subtype). When the sample method creates the array, it uses the class of the first element - an anonymous subclass of Object - for the array's component type. However, sample() may return another Object subtype (or the base Object), which cannot be stored in the array of the first singleton's type.

Hence, the core problem is that the array is created with the exact runtime class of the first singleton element instead of a class guaranteed to be assignable from all sample results. This violates Java array type safety and triggers an exception when storing samples of different but compatible types.

The failing test reproduces this by having distinct anonymous class instances for keys, leading to the exception when the sample method creates an array from the first singleton's class and tries to store potentially other types.

# Next step

Identify the method c0.m0(int) in the issue report to check if it corresponds to sample(int) and confirm this problem in the code. Then consider fixes such as changing array creation to use the generic type T's class or returning a collection instead of an array to avoid the problem.

messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis

Details:
The failure originates in the DiscreteDistribution class, especially in the sample(int) method. This method creates an array of type T with the component type set as the runtime class of the first element of the 'singletons' list.

The key lines leading to failure are:

```java
final T[] out = (T[]) java.lang.reflect.Array.newInstance(singletons.get(0).getClass(), sampleSize);
for (int i = 0; i < sampleSize; i++) {
    out[i] = sample();
}
```

The problem occurs if `singletons.get(0)` is of a subtype T1 of T, but sample() returns instances of base type T or a different subtype. Since the array was created specifically for T1, inserting T objects that are not of T1 throws ArrayStoreException.

The constructor of DiscreteDistribution stores the keys (the discrete support points) into the singletons list. In the failing test, these keys are anonymous subclasses of Object (each call to `new Object() {}` produces a unique anonymous subclass), so the class of the first entry is a different anonymous class than the class of the second entry.

The sample() method selects an element from singletons according to probability distributions and therefore can produce elements of a different anonymous subclass than the first singleton. This array type mismatch leads to the exception.

Thus, the root cause is that the array's component type is obtained from only the first element's exact runtime class without considering the static type T or the heterogeneity of the elements in 'singletons'. This is inherently unsafe as the sample method may produce a value incompatible with the array component type.

The failing test reproduces this by creating a list of pairs with two different anonymous Object subclasses and calls sample(1) expecting an array of length 1.

Summary: Using `singletons.get(0).getClass()` to create the array is unsafe and can lead to ArrayStoreException if sampled objects at runtime are not of the same runtime class as the first singleton.

This matches the bug report's summary and explains why the exception happens during `sample(int)` in this scenario.

# Next step:

If the generic type's exact Class object is available, use it for array creation. Otherwise, consider returning an Object[] or List<T> or other collection that avoids array creation based on the runtime class of an element.

Proposed fix locations would be the sample(int) method in DiscreteDistribution.
